# How many ElevenLabs credits does a 10-minute narration actually use?

Disclosure: This article contains an affiliate link. Anicca is an independent ElevenLabs affiliate and may earn a commission if you subscribe through it, at no extra cost to you.

The pricing page answers this question in minutes — roughly 10 minutes on Free, roughly 30 on Starter, roughly 121 on Creator. That answer is only true if every credit goes to text to speech, and if your script happens to match the page's implied rate. We checked the official pricing page on 9 November 2026 and worked through the arithmetic ourselves, because the unit ElevenLabs actually charges in is not minutes. It is characters. Once you count characters, the right plan for a narration project stops being a guess.

## What is a credit, in ElevenLabs' own pricing?

On the pricing page we checked on 9 November 2026, all products draw from one shared monthly credit pool. For text to speech with the V2 Multilingual models, one text character costs one credit. Some Flash and Turbo models cost less per character for API use — between 0.5 and 1 credit per character, according to the same page — but the standard web workflow is easiest to budget at one credit per character.

The other products draw from the same pool at very different rates. The pricing page lists speech to text at about 330 credits per minute, music at about 900 credits per minute, voice changer and voice isolator at about 1,000 credits per minute, and dubbing at between 2,000 and 10,000 credits per minute depending on the mode. That shared pool is the fact the headline minute figures hide: ten minutes of voice isolation costs about as many credits as a 10,000-character narration.

## Why should you count characters instead of minutes?

Minutes depend on how fast a voice reads, how many pauses your script contains, and how much of the finished piece is music or silence. Characters are sitting in your document right now, and you can count them exactly before you spend anything. Your text editor's character count — including spaces and punctuation, as typed — is the number that predicts your spend.

There is a useful check hidden in the pricing page itself. Its comparison table lists roughly 10, 30, 121 and 600 included minutes for Free, Starter, Creator and Pro, against pools of 10,000, 30,000, 121,000 and 600,000 credits. The minutes are simply the credits divided by 1,000, which tells you the page assumes roughly 1,000 characters of script per finished minute. If your scripts run denser than that, your minutes will run out faster than the table suggests. If they run lighter, you will get more.

## A worked example: one narration, counted honestly

Take a single narration project with a finished script of 9,200 characters, counted in the document before generation. Here is what it actually costs at one credit per character:

- One full generation of the script: 9,200 credits.
- Two retakes of one 600-character section that did not sound right: 1,200 credits.
- One full regeneration after a script edit: another 9,200 credits.
- Total for one finished piece: 19,600 credits.

That total is the honest number, and it changes the plan decision. The Free pool of 10,000 credits does not cover one finished piece of this size once retakes and a single edit are included — it covers the first full generation and little else, which makes Free a test of voice fit, not a production plan. The Starter pool of 30,000 credits covers this piece with 10,400 credits to spare. The Creator pool of 121,000 credits covers about six pieces of this size in a month, before anything else touches the pool.

Now add one other product. If you also clean a 10-minute voice recording with the voice isolator at about 1,000 credits per minute, that is roughly another 10,000 credits — the equivalent of a second full narration script. A Starter month that looked comfortable can be spent by one narration project plus one cleanup job. This is why budgeting per product, in credits, is the only version of the maths that survives contact with a real project.

## What did the plans cost on the day we checked?

These are the monthly prices and credit pools shown on the official pricing page on 9 November 2026. Prices exclude taxes, levies and duties, and the page showed time-limited first-month offers — Starter at $1 for the first month and Creator at $11 for the first month, both marked as ending 16 November — so treat the first-month figures as a promotion, not the price of the plan.

- Free: $0 per month, 10,000 credits.
- Starter: $6 per month after the first month, 30,000 credits.
- Creator: $22 per month after the first month, 121,000 credits.
- Pro: $99 per month, 600,000 credits.
- Scale: $299 per month, 1.8 million credits.
- Business: $990 per month, 6 million credits.

The step that matters for most solo narration work is Free to Starter — not because of the extra 20,000 credits, but because, as our earlier guide to [ElevenLabs plans for solo creators](/blog/elevenlabs-plans-for-solo-creators) explains, a paid plan is also where commercial usage rights begin. If you publish or monetise the output, that rights question comes before the credit question.

## How should you budget your own first project?

Count the characters in the script you actually intend to record, including spaces. Multiply by two — one full generation, plus the retakes and one regeneration that real projects almost always need. Then add any non-narration work at its own rate: minutes of transcription at about 330 credits each, minutes of voice cleanup at about 1,000 credits each, minutes of dubbing at 2,000 credits and up. Compare that total, not the headline minutes, with the plan pools above.

If the total sits far below 10,000, test on Free first and spend nothing — that is the sequence we recommend in [how to test an AI voice tool before you pay](/blog/how-to-test-ai-voice-tools-before-you-pay). If it sits between 10,000 and 30,000, Starter is the working plan. If you are producing several finished pieces a month, do the same count for a whole month before assuming Creator is headroom rather than necessity.

[Try ElevenLabs free](https://try.elevenlabs.io/elevenlabs-en-1) on your own script first, and compare the credit balance before and after one real generation with your character count. That single measurement — your script, your voice settings, your retakes — is worth more than any minute estimate, including ours.

## Common questions

### Does a retake cost credits?

Yes. Every generation spends credits per character generated, so regenerating a section spends that section's characters again. Budgeting a multiplier for retakes, as in the worked example above, is how you avoid a pool that runs out mid-project.

### Do unused credits roll over?

The pricing page we checked describes the pools as monthly credits. Treat them as a monthly budget and check the current terms on the pricing page before relying on any rollover behaviour for a large project.

### Is text to speech the cheapest way to spend credits?

Per unit, yes, at one credit per character for the standard models. Transcription, music, voice cleanup and especially dubbing spend the same pool hundreds or thousands of credits per minute, so mixed workflows drain a plan far faster than narration alone.

### Which plan should a solo creator start with?

Start with Free to test voice fit on your own material. Move to Starter when you need commercial usage rights or when your counted project total passes 10,000 credits. Move up only when a counted month of real work — not a headline minute figure — says the smaller pool is the bottleneck.
